entries.title: Matt Pocock's dictionary splits hallucinations into factuality and faithfulness
entries.summary: A glossary entry from Matt Pocock's AI Coding Dictionary splits hallucination into two kinds. Factuality errors come from missing knowledge and are fixed by adding context; faithfulness errors come from attention degradation on loaded context and are fixed by clearing or compacting. It argues that misdiagnosing faithfulness as factuality makes things worse, because pasting more docs grows the context.

lessons.point: The fix for the two kinds is opposite: add context for missing knowledge, remove context for drift from knowledge already loaded.

lessons.point: Before adding docs, check whether the correct information was already in context; if it was, the problem is faithfulness, not missing knowledge.
lessons.excerpt: check whether the correct information was already in context before deciding which problem you have

lessons.point: Hallucinated code looks plausible by construction, so it tends to pass a quick review and fail only when run.
lessons.excerpt: Hallucinated code is plausible by construction

entries.takeaway: A useful diagnostic framing for coding agents (add context vs compact), stated as opinion with no data.

actionable.detail: When a coding agent invents an API, first grep the current context or session for the correct signature. If it is present, compact or clear and reload instead of pasting more documentation; if absent, load the docs or type definitions.

entries.title: Simon Willison folds agent-written PR descriptions under a human summary

lessons.excerpt: An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive.

lessons.point: The full agent-written text is kept, but collapsed, so nothing is lost for reviewers who want it.

entries.title: METR proposes third-party review of unreleased models by mining internal transcripts
entries.summary: METR outlines how a third-party assessor would estimate the worst misaligned actions a developer's agents could take, by surveying incidents across training, evaluations and internal use and testing whether those incidents understate the risk. The behaviors in scope include hacking external parties, tampering with logs, colluding against monitors, exfiltrating weights and acquiring resources beyond the task. METR says its Hugging Face incident investigation cost about $400K in API credits over six days, and it estimates a rigorous two-month assessment would cost over $10M.

entries.title: Flide is an inference engine that serves Jev-style decision models faster
entries.summary: Flide is an Apache-2.0 inference engine for Jev-style decision models. It serves the `/v1/systemone` API and forks one encoded state into several questions. entries.title: MLX tensor parallelism over Thunderbolt serves a mixture-of-experts model on Mac Studios
entries.summary: Apple benchmarks the MLX framework on Mac Studio with Qwen 3.8 (27B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128B) and Muse Spark Open (816B mixture of experts, run in 4-bit NVFP4 format). Moving from a single M3 Ultra to a single M5 Ultra gives up to 4.6x faster time to first token (TTFT) and 1.6x faster decode. Splitting a model across 2 or 4 machines over RDMA (remote direct memory access) on Thunderbolt 5 adds further speedups, and four machines run Muse Spark Open at 36.73 tokens/s. Apple shows serving with mlx_lm.server and pointing the OpenCode coding agent at that server's OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

entries.title: Claude Code's Ultracode subagents worked 12+ hours from a one-line prompt
entries.summary: Simon Willison ran Claude Code for web in Ultracode mode, where Claude Code writes JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents. A one-line phone prompt containing a typo led to over 12 hours of work and a multi-crate Rust SQLite extension for SPARQL 1.1, a query language for RDF graph data. It passes 636 of 639 applicable W3C conformance tests and reports 3.5x speedups in count mode (2.8x returning full results) over translating SPARQL to SQL. Willison says reviewing the code is not feasible, and questions the value of a large artifact nobody will invest time to understand.
entries.takeaway: Large subagent workflows can finish big, test-backed builds without supervision, so the bottleneck moves to human review; plan for verification artifacts such as conformance suites, differential fuzzing and documentation up front.

lessons.point: Ultracode orchestrates by generating code: the agent writes JavaScript that defines its own subagent network.
lessons.excerpt: it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems.

lessons.point: A one-line phone prompt with a typo was enough to start a 12-hour run.
lessons.excerpt: This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours.

lessons.point: The W3C conformance results were the main quality signal reported for code nobody reviewed.
lessons.excerpt: passing 636 of 639 applicable W3C evaluation tests

lessons.point: The author questions the value of output nobody can or will understand.
lessons.excerpt: how valuable is that if I created it on a whim

actionable.title: Define verification before launching a long subagent run
actionable.detail: Before starting a multi-hour orchestrated run, name the oracle the output will be judged against, such as a standard conformance suite, differential fuzzing against a reference implementation, or a benchmark. Require per-component READMEs and a tutorial in the initial prompt, not as a follow-up, so the result can be evaluated without reading all the code.

entries.title: SpecForge compiles team rules into checks that agents cannot skip
entries.author: leaderiop
entries.summary: SpecForge is a Rust compiler that turns small .spec files into a typed, checked graph of entities and rules, and refuses any edit that breaks a rule, whether a person or an agent made it. Agents reach it over MCP, a CLI or LSP. Its pitch is that prompts and skill files are 'soft skills' an agent can silently ignore, while deterministic checks are 'hard skills' it cannot.
entries.takeaway: Move the rules an agent must obey out of the prompt and into a deterministic check that fails, the same way tests gate code.

lessons.point: Rules written as prose in the agent's context can be skipped without any signal.
lessons.excerpt:
A **soft skill** is advice placed in the AI's context: a prompt, a Markdown spec, a policy PDF, a skill file. It
helps, but it's prose. The AI may follow it, or not.

lessons.point: A program-enforced rule fails loudly and gives the same verdict every time.
lessons.excerpt: A **hard skill** is a rule a program enforces. The AI can't skip it, because the check fails and says why.

actionable.title: Turn each must-follow rule in your agent prompt into a check that blocks
actionable.detail: List the rules in your CLAUDE.md or skill files that must never be broken, and enforce each one with a hook, linter, schema validator or CI check that fails with a reason; keep the prose only as a hint.

entries.prior_art: Policy-as-code (OPA/Rego), schema validation, and harness hooks that block tool calls; spec-driven development tools such as Kiro and spec-kit.

entries.title: Google's VERID checks agent-written lab-robot protocols against a 3D digital twin
entries.summary: VERID, built on PyLabRobot, is a live digital twin of a lab workcell that tracks geometry, well volumes, reagents and tips, dry-runs protocols, and blocks invalid commands before they reach liquid-handling robots. In aptamer design loops, agents optimizing raw binding on myoglobin enriched non-specific G-quadruplex binders, and specificity fell from 75.0% to 19.1%. The agents revised their design rules and reached a 33.5% on-target hit rate; in protein binder design, scientist-plus-agent collaboration nearly doubled the in-silico hit rate of a scientist working alone at equal compute.
entries.takeaway: Agent actions on the physical world need validation against live state, not just syntax, and agents optimizing a proxy metric will exploit artifacts until real-world readouts expose them.

lessons.point: Code that passes syntax checks can still be impossible or invalid given live physical state. Validation needs a stateful model of the environment.
lessons.excerpt: An agent can generate syntactically valid code that is physically impossible

lessons.point: A mandatory dry run in simulation, plus validation against the digital twin, acts as a gate between agent output and actuators.
lessons.excerpt: agents never send unverified code directly to the liquid handling robots. Every protocol is dry-run in simulation and validated against the digital twin before touching reagents.

lessons.point: Optimizing a proxy (raw pull-down) produced artifacts that cut the bead-corrected hit rate from 10.2% to 3.7% until wet-lab data exposed them.
lessons.excerpt: causing both target specificity (from 75.0% to 19.1%) and true, bead-corrected hit rate (from 10.2% to 3.7%) to plunge.

lessons.point: Splitting work so humans set strategy and agents handle tactics nearly doubled the in-silico hit rate of a scientist working alone at equal compute.
lessons.excerpt: human–agent collaboration, where a scientist sets the high-level strategy and an agent drives tactical execution, nearly doubled the in-silico hit rate of a scientist working alone

actionable.title: Gate physical or high-impact agent actions behind a stateful simulator
actionable.detail: Keep a live model of the environment state that the agent can query before acting. Dry-run every agent-generated plan against it. Reject commands that are impossible or invalid given the current state, and feed the rejection back so the agent can replan. Log synchronized execution traces for debugging. Track the true objective alongside any proxy metric the agent optimizes, so you can catch it gaming the proxy.

entries.verify_note: First verifier refuted 'agents caught' (wet-lab data exposed the failure) and a missing in-silico qualifier; rewritten, and a fresh verifier found every figure supported. Verifier novelty 40, relevance 45.
entries.prior_art: The nearest pool entry is 'Scientific computing in the age of agentic AI' (ai-research), which covers agents in science broadly. This item adds a concrete pattern of validating actions against a digital twin before they reach robots. It also adds measured closed-loop results, including an observed proxy-metric failure and the agents' recovery from it. It is mostly applied science, and the harness pattern is what transfers.

entries.title: OpenAI launches the Agents API in public beta, a hosted Codex harness
entries.summary: OpenAI offers the harness behind Codex as a managed service. A single call specifies task, model, tools and environment, and the sandbox can be OpenAI-hosted, self-hosted or from partners such as E2B, Modal and Cloudflare. The harness handles automatic compaction, tool search, programmatic tool calling and parallel subagents, and costs only the tokens and tools used. This is a product launch with no measurements.

lessons.point: The vendor runs the harness while you pick where the agent's code executes.
lessons.excerpt: OpenAI hosts and maintains the harness. You choose the agent’s compute environment: in an OpenAI-managed sandbox, on your own infrastructure, or with one of our sandbox partners.

lessons.point: Compaction is handled by the platform, so long sessions can span several context windows.
lessons.excerpt: Developers can build workflows that span multiple context windows without implementing their own compaction logic.

lessons.point: Subagents are used to keep each worker's context focused.
lessons.excerpt: Each subagent maintains its own context, helping it stay focused on its assignment, while the main agent coordinates their work and brings the results together.

lessons.point: MCP and custom tools are supported, so tool trust is still the developer's responsibility.
lessons.excerpt: The Agents API supports MCP, custom functions, and built-in tools like web search.

entries.takeaway: A managed harness removes orchestration work but shifts trust to the vendor's harness and to whichever sandbox and tools you attach.

actionable.title: Decide sandbox placement and tool trust before adopting a hosted agent harness
actionable.detail: When evaluating a hosted agent API, list which sandbox option (vendor-managed, your virtual private cloud (VPC) or a partner) holds your files and secrets, which MCP servers and custom functions the agent can call, and how compaction summaries are logged. Pilot on a low-risk task during the public beta.

entries.title: SWT-Bench is a Docker harness that scores LLM-written tests reproducing GitHub issues
entries.summary: SWT-Bench re-uses SWE-bench tooling and datasets, but asks the model for a reproducing test instead of a fix. The test must fail on the original code and pass once a patch resolving the issue is applied. The harness has two modes: unit tests run in the project's suite, or standalone reproduction scripts judged only by exit code. It also reports coverage change and ships Lite (276), Verified (433) and Full (2294) datasets.

lessons.point: A good test for a bug report fails on the unpatched code and passes on the patched code. You can use the same check to verify agent-written reproduction tests in your own pipeline.
lessons.excerpt: a language model is tasked with generating a *reproducing test* that fails in the original state of the code base and passes after a patch resolving the issue has been applied.

lessons.point: Reproduction-script mode judges success only by the script's exit code. It does not run the project's existing test suite.
lessons.excerpt: The evaluation harness runs the script on the codebase and determines success based on the script's exit code: 0 for pass and 1 for fail.

lessons.point: Clean up agent leftovers before scoring. For OpenHands, the authors discarded all top-level files to remove stale reproduction scripts the agent wrote.
lessons.excerpt: For our evaluation of OpenHands, we automatically discard all top-level files to remove stale reproduction scripts generated by the agent.

entries.takeaway: If your coding agent claims it reproduced a bug, require a test that fails before the fix and passes after. SWT-Bench is a ready-made harness for measuring how often it can.

actionable.title: Add a fail-before, pass-after gate for agent-written reproduction tests
actionable.detail: Run each agent-written reproduction test twice: on the base commit, where it must fail, and on the patched commit, where it must pass. Also run the existing suite to catch tests that break it. Before scoring, remove stray top-level scripts the agent left behind. To compare against published agents, run your model on SWT-Bench Lite (276 instances).

entries.prior_art: SWT-Bench is a 2024 NeurIPS paper built on the SWE-bench harness; the README adds no new results. The nearest pool items are the swe-bench-doesnt-generalize-to-production-tasks claim and eval-methodology entries; none cover fail-to-pass reproduction tests.
entries.verify_note: Verifier: excerpts verbatim and dataset sizes correct, but the draft over-reached (author attribution, regression-catching inference, filler lesson). Text corrected; held as an old 2024 benchmark README with low novelty.

entries.title: MentalHealthBench scores model replies against weighted expert-consensus rubrics
entries.summary: OpenAI released an open benchmark of synthetic mental health conversations, from everyday stress to emergencies, across adults, teens, caregivers and clinicians. Over 80 licensed experts wrote per-conversation rubric items weighted from -10 to +10, and only items that at least two of three reviewers agreed on were kept. A model grader scores replies against these rubrics, and the score can be split into ten behavior dimensions, so models with the same total can show different strengths.

lessons.point: Per-conversation rubric items carry signed weights, so harmful behavior is penalized and clinically important behavior counts more, rather than a single pass/fail.
lessons.excerpt: They each carry a weight ranging from -10 to +10: positive points reward beneficial behaviors, while negative points penalize harmful ones

lessons.point: Rubric quality control uses a simple consensus rule: keep an item only if two of three experts agree and none contradicts it.
lessons.excerpt: we only retained criteria agreed upon by at least two experts and not contradicted by a third

lessons.point: Breaking the total score into behavior dimensions reveals differences that a single headline number hides.
lessons.excerpt: Models with similar overall scores can have different strengths across these behaviors.

lessons.point: Users and experts value different things: users weight practical next steps and tone, experts weight context-gathering. The benchmark scores only the expert view.
lessons.excerpt: User perspectives highlighted qualities people value in AI support that were less emphasized in expert guidance, particularly practical next steps and tone.

entries.takeaway: For subjective, high-stakes domains, weighted per-scenario rubrics with an expert-agreement filter and dimension-level scoring give a more usable eval than a single safety pass rate.

actionable.title: Build domain evals as weighted per-scenario rubrics with an agreement filter
actionable.detail: For each eval scenario, have 3 domain reviewers write single-aspect criteria with signed weights (e.g. -10..+10); keep only criteria at least 2 agree on and none contradicts; grade with a model judge against those criteria and report per-dimension scores alongside the total, not just the headline number.

entries.prior_art: OpenAI HealthBench (same expert-rubric plus model-grader method).

entries.title: Context-Regularized Cross-Entropy makes image classifiers rely less on background context
entries.summary: Image classifiers often break when an object shows up against a background they did not see in training. This is called context shift. The authors first build a more faithful attribution method, ContrastiveCAMs (a variant of class activation maps). They then use it in a new training loss, Context-Regularized Cross-Entropy (CR-CE), which reduces how much the model attends to context regions. They report consistent robustness gains on Waterbirds, Spawrious, ImageNet/ImageNet-BG and Hard-ImageNet.

lessons.point: Existing feature-attribution methods have a theoretical limitation, so the authors propose ContrastiveCAMs to get more faithful attribution maps.
lessons.excerpt: we introduce a new variant, ContrastiveCAMs, which produces more faithful attribution maps of model predictions

lessons.point: CR-CE changes the standard cross-entropy loss so the model's attention to contextual regions is suppressed during training.
lessons.excerpt: a modification of the standard cross-entropy loss that regularizes the model's attention by suppressing the influence of contextual regions

lessons.point: The authors claim consistent robustness gains across several datasets. The abstract gives no numbers.
lessons.excerpt: and report consistent improvements in context-shift robustness

entries.takeaway: This is a vision-training result about spurious background cues in convolutional neural networks (CNNs), with no direct use for LLM harness or agent builders.

actionable.title: Record only; relevant to teams training vision classifiers
actionable.detail: If you train convolutional image classifiers that fail on unfamiliar backgrounds, test CR-CE on a held-out benchmark with shifted backgrounds, such as Waterbirds or ImageNet-BG. Compare it against plain cross-entropy before adopting it. LLM agent pipelines need no action.

entries.verify_note: Abstract-only source; claims match, datasets correct.
entries.prior_art: Right for the Right Reasons (Ross et al. 2017), CAM-guided training such as GAIN, Waterbirds/GroupDRO, ImageNet background-challenge work

entries.title: Gradium releases Phonon, a small on-device text-to-speech model
entries.summary: Gradium released Phonon, a small text-to-speech (TTS) model that runs fully on the device with no server or network. entries.title: Workshop paper proposes retrieval as local traversal through a memory address space
entries.summary: The authors separate a memory's content from its address. They frame retrieval as a persistent walk through nearby addresses, with an indexing objective that charges for each memory made reachable. Only the simplest fixed-geometry version is tested, on the MiniGrid Memory task. There, a traversal head reached 0.95 mean return in 0.59M training steps, versus 0.94M for Gaussian absolute addressing and more than 2M for categorical absolute addressing.

lessons.point: The core design move is to decouple what a memory contains from where it sits, so geometry controls only retrieval cost.
lessons.excerpt: We separate a memory's content from its address.

lessons.point: The objective pushes complementary memories together and keeps redundant ones apart, even when each is useful on its own.
lessons.excerpt: redundant memories should not occupy the same retrieval set solely because they are individually useful

lessons.point: In the toy experiment, stateful traversal learned faster than absolute addressing.
lessons.excerpt: A persistent local traversal head reaches 0.95mean return after 0.59M training steps with a five-token context

lessons.point: The evidence is a proof of principle only. Learned geometry and repeated retrieval were not tested.
lessons.excerpt: The experiment does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval.

entries.takeaway: This is an early architecture hypothesis that stateful retrieval is easier to learn than stateless retrieval, not something harness builders can use yet.

actionable.title: Watch for a full evaluation before acting
actionable.detail: No harness change is warranted. Revisit if follow-up work tests learned geometry and repeated retrieval on language tasks rather than MiniGrid.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: lessons match the paper; it is a single-task proof of principle, which the entry already says.
entries.prior_art: The nearest pool entries are about agent-level memory, such as LiveMem (memory state continuity in long-running inference) and Hugging Face funes (raw-session memory). Nothing in the pool covers learned address-space traversal heads, so the novelty is mid but sits outside the pool's harness focus.

entries.title: A Thomson Reuters engineer runs a coding agent fully offline with Qwen
entries.summary: A principal engineer at Thomson Reuters shows how to run the OpenCode coding agent with no internet, using Ollama to serve Qwen3.5 9B on a laptop. The configuration enables only the local provider, asks before file edits and shell commands, and blocks web tools. Offline, the agent fixed a one-line bug and the existing tests passed, which the author checked by re-running them. The author says this shows only that small, self-contained tasks work, not how the setup copes with large repositories.

lessons.point: Anything that needs the network, such as new packages or web lookups, has to be prepared before going offline.
lessons.excerpt: Downloading a new package or looking something up on the web will still need a connection.

lessons.point: The small local model guessed the wrong test runner once, so put the exact test command in the prompt.
lessons.excerpt: For the next task, I would include the exact test command in the prompt: python3 -m unittest -v.

lessons.point: Existing, unchanged tests give the agent a target and give you a check that does not depend on the agent's own explanation.
lessons.excerpt: It also gives us a way to check the result independently of its explanation.

lessons.point: Lock the local setup down: local provider only, approval before edits and commands, web tools blocked.
lessons.excerpt: It also asks before editing files or running shell commands, and blocks the web tools.

entries.takeaway: A 9B local model with OpenCode can handle small, test-backed fixes offline, but the source shows only one trivial task.

actionable.title: Set up an offline OpenCode plus Ollama coding agent
actionable.detail: While still online, start Ollama with OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:11434 OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=65536 ollama serve and run ollama pull qwen3.5:9b. In opencode.json, point baseURL at http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1, enable only the local provider, require approval for edits and shell commands, and block web tools. Launch with opencode --pure once online, then disconnect. Give the exact test command in every prompt and re-run the tests yourself afterwards. Budget 12-16 GB of RAM or more for a 64k context.

entries.title: SAFT adversarially trains only robustness-critical parameters and beats LoRA
entries.summary: Adversarial training (AT) makes neural networks robust to small adversarial input perturbations, but it is memory-heavy on large models. LoRA-based AT leaves a robustness gap compared with full-parameter AT. The authors find that adversarial gradients concentrate on a small set of "Robustness-Critical Parameters". Sparse Adversarial Fine-Tuning (SAFT) updates only those, about 5% of parameters, and the abstract says it approaches or surpasses full AT on robustness.

lessons.point: Low-rank adapters cost robustness compared with full-parameter adversarial training.
lessons.excerpt: this constraint induces a notable robustness gap relative to full-parameter AT

lessons.point: Gradient analysis suggests robustness lives in a sparse subset of weights.

entries.title: Researchers' VA-TDM method improves four-step image and video diffusion generation
entries.summary: Diffusion models normally need many sampling steps. Distillation trains a 'student' model to produce similar output in only a few steps. lessons.point: Score-distillation methods can be misled at intermediate steps, because their estimators may track a different distribution from the one that updates the student.
lessons.excerpt: commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student.

lessons.point: A learned critic over velocity fields gives one framework that covers several existing distillation objectives.
lessons.excerpt: VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives.

entries.takeaway: This off-thesis diffusion research matters only if you serve image or video generation and want fewer sampling steps.

entries.title: Workshop paper proposes retrieval as a local walk through memory

entries.title: Survey maps how self-improving AI systems can fake gains or lose safeguards
entries.summary: A new survey defines recursive self-improvement as AI systems changing their own models, prompts, memories, tools and update mechanisms, and groups the requirements for doing it safely into four themes: genuine improvement, behavioral constraints and alignment, security and privacy, and transparency and controllability. It warns that reported gains can come from flawed evaluations, that compromised artifacts can carry into successor systems, and that changing the improvement process can invalidate earlier verification. It is a literature review with no new experiments.

lessons.point: Self-reported gains can be evaluation artifacts, and old capabilities and constraints can erode.
lessons.excerpt: Reported gains may reflect flawed evaluations, previously acquired capabilities may deteriorate, and compliance with behavioral constraints may weaken.

lessons.point: Compromised artifacts can carry into later versions of a self-updating system.
lessons.excerpt: Compromised artifacts or sensitive information may also persist in successor systems.

lessons.point: Changing how the system improves can void earlier verification.
lessons.excerpt: Changes to improvement mechanisms may invalidate earlier verification results and make human oversight less effective.

entries.takeaway: If your agent rewrites its own prompts, memory or tools, re-verify after each change against a held-out evaluation it cannot edit.

actionable.title: Gate self-modifying agents on a frozen held-out evaluation
actionable.detail: When an agent edits its own prompts, skills, memory or tools, keep a held-out evaluation set and scoring code outside its write access, re-run it after every accepted change, and keep the previous version to roll back to.

entries.title: HybridAgent reasons in latent space and calls tools in text

lessons.excerpt: HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text

entries.title: Daniel Miessler frames AI work as hill-climbing against ideal-state evals
entries.summary: Daniel Miessler argues that most AI work follows one loop. You state your purpose, write down the ideal state, turn it into evals, let AI do the work, then iterate on both the output and the evals. He claims the main limit today is how clearly people say what they want, not what AI can do. The essay lists eval types, from plain code checks to repeated runs and judges tuned on your past ratings, and it has no experiments.

lessons.point: Miessler claims stating the goal clearly, not AI execution, is now the main constraint.
lessons.excerpt: the primary limitation for AI today is not its ability to build what you ask for. It's your ability to clearly articulate what you want.

lessons.point: If output passes every eval but you still dislike it, the evals need updating.
lessons.excerpt: The best way to tell if you need to update your evals is if you get a result that perfectly passes your evals, but you still don't like it for some reason.

lessons.point: Evals should include actually running the thing and repeated trials, not a single pass.
lessons.excerpt: Does it hold up every time? (running it ten times and seeing how many pass, not just once)

entries.takeaway: Treat the written ideal state as the source of your verification criteria, and update the evals whenever passing output still feels wrong.

entries.title: Bound-conditioned latent inference cuts progressive image codec BD-rate on Kodak
entries.summary: Progressive image codecs send one bitstream that can be cut short at any point, encoding latents as trit-planes (base-3 digit layers). This NeurIPS 2026 paper treats the trits decoded so far as lower and upper bounds on each continuous latent, and uses the center and width of those bounds to refine both the entropy model and the reconstruction. On Kodak it lowers BD-rate (the average bitrate saving at equal quality) by 17.78% vs DPICT and 7.96% vs CTC, using one shared model instead of per-plane predictors.

lessons.point: Decoded trits are used as interval constraints on continuous latents, not only as discrete symbols.
lessons.excerpt: reformulates progressive trit-plane coding as sequential latent inference under shrinking interval constraints

lessons.point: The method beats prior progressive codecs on rate-distortion on Kodak.
lessons.excerpt: reducing BD-rate by 17.78%over DPICT and by 7.96%over CTC on Kodak

lessons.point: One shared model replaces plane-specific predictors, cutting parameters and latency.
lessons.excerpt: replacing CTC's plane-specific predictors with a shared model that uses about 5.3×fewer parameters and achieves lower latency than CTC

entries.takeaway: A solid image-compression result, but it has no bearing on securing or building AI agents and harnesses.

entries.title: RoboCasa-Shift shows equal success-rate drops in a VLA policy hide different failures
entries.summary: RoboCasa-Shift is a robustness benchmark for vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies. It pairs each clean rollout with a perturbed one that differs only in one shift, and records which task stage fails. Testing GR00T N1.5 over 1,040 rollouts, it finds that headline success rate hides a lot: one camera shift left success unchanged while 8 of 80 paired episodes flipped outcome, and two shifts with the same success drop failed at the first stage at very different rates (19.0% vs 36.4%).

lessons.point: Matched clean/perturbed pairs isolate the effect of one shift per comparison.
lessons.excerpt: matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift

lessons.point: Higher perturbation severity does not reliably mean worse performance, so severity sweeps need care.
lessons.excerpt: Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation.

lessons.point: The same aggregate drop can come from failures at different depths of execution.
lessons.excerpt: Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles.

entries.takeaway: Aggregate success rate can hide outcome flips and which task stage fails; the study covers one robot policy on four simulated tasks.

actionable.title: Report paired flip rates and stage of failure alongside success rate in long-horizon evals
actionable.detail: When testing an agent under a perturbation, run matched clean/perturbed pairs with the same seed and settings, count outcome flips in both directions (not just the net success delta), and log the first sub-step that failed so equal drops can be told apart.

entries.prior_art: Extends RoboCasa365 and general VLA robustness benchmarks that report aggregate task success; the eval-methodology point echoes the tracker claim that headline benchmark metrics can mask distinct failure modes. entries.title: Hugging Face launches an Open TTS Leaderboard ranking open text-to-speech models
entries.summary: Hugging Face built a TTS leaderboard that scores models with automatic metrics. Word error rate comes from an automatic speech recognition (ASR) model's transcript. entries.title: Venus-DefakerOne2 detects image and video forgeries with one forensics model
entries.summary: Venus-DefakerOne2 is a vision-forensics foundation model trained on tens of millions of open-source and in-house samples. It makes a single real-or-fake decision across deepfake faces, AI-generated images and videos, tampered documents, manipulated natural images, and physical spoofs. The paper credits two techniques: Tide-Style-Tuning, which alternates low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and full-parameter fine-tuning, and entropy-based test-time selection of the prediction modality. It reports top scores from 87.6% on tampered documents to 96.7% on deepfake faces.
entries.takeaway: It is a candidate forgery detector for fraud and identity teams, and has little bearing on agent or harness work.

lessons.point: At inference, the model picks which modality's prediction to trust based on how uncertain each prediction is.
lessons.excerpt: Entropy-based Test Adaptation determines the optimal prediction modality by analyzing prediction entropy.
